2.text: also from starvation, and could hardly reach the shores of the Anadyr again.

3.text: To the same year, 1763, belong three other reports,¹ taken down, one from

4.text: Chukchee visitors to the Anadyr River; another from a Cossack who was

5.text: taken captive by the Reindeer Chukchee and spent about two years with

6.text: them; and the third from a captive woman, a native of America, who was

7.text: taken by the islanders when ten years old, then sold to Reindeer Chukchee for

8.text: an iron-headed spear and two white fawn-skins, and by her last owner given

9.text: to a Cossack of Anadyr in exchange for a copper kettle. All these reports

10.text: contain interesting details concerning the Chukchee and also about America.

11.text: Regarding the Chukchee, the Russian captive mentions that he has seen how

12.text: a father killed his son, and a brother killed another brother. Then he describes

13.text: how the Yukaghir of the Anadyr came to the Chukchee to ransom off their

14.text: captives. The Yukaghir brought tobacco, kettles, knives, axes, bows and

15.text: arrows, and beads. They ransomed off nine people. The Chukchee were quite

16.text: contented, and gave to the Yukaghir fawn-skin coats, white fawn-skins, white

17.text: reindeer-leg skins, coats of marten-skin, red foxes. As to America, the Chukchee

18.text: visitor, in the first report, mentions that the people living there are called

19.text: Kykhmyn.² They have needles of copper. This copper is red, and they get

20.text: it in their own country, but in which way they procure it he does not know.

21.text: In the winter and in the spring those American people arrange large hunts

22.text: for wild reindeer. They cut down for this purpose large abatis and arrange

23.text: fences so that the reindeer are caught by thousands. They bring sacrifices

24.text: to the sun and to the sea, saying, “I give you here a sacrifice from my labor.

25.text: You also be my assistant in my need” (this short incantation is quite Chukchee,

26.text: both in sense and in style).³

27.text: The captive woman said that the American people had houses made of

28.text: green wood, poplar, larch, and aspen, beam to beam standing aslant. Their

29.text: form is round. They are covered with earth. The summer lodges are also

30.text: of round form, covered with reindeer-skins and walrus-hide. The store-rooms

31.text: are dug into the ground. The people have no iron, with the exception of a

32.text: few iron knives bought from the Chukchee. They obtain fire by striking one

33.text: stone against another. They cook their food in earthen pots manufactured

35.text: It may not be out of place to mention here several expeditions of

36.text: Demetrius Laptev, the marine lieutenant who in 1739-42 surveyed the Arctic

37.text: coast from the Lena River to the Large Baranov Cape, though his expeditions

38.text: were purely scientific, and had no reference to Chukchee wars. Laptev, with

41.note: Two comparanda glossed explicitly as non-English forms (R8: no Chukchee priors apply to the Eskimo form). First term Kɪˊɪmɪn matches lexicon key Ki_'i_mi_n (ref 1-041 l.17, 3-072 l.27) exactly as printed, keyed as {Ki_'i_mi_n}. Second term, glossed "Asiatic Eskimo", read at 4x as Kiˊxmi with plain lowercase dotted i and no macron; the lexicon's ratified form for this word (key Ki='xmi, ref 1-041 l.40-41) is Kīˊxmi with a macron over the first i. This occurrence's print does not show that macron under 4x magnification, so it is keyed as printed (Kiˊxmi) rather than with the handle, per the instruction to key what disagrees and note it.
